sections.name: Chip Fabrication
sections.blurb:
This section covers the companies that physically manufacture AI silicon, on which process nodes, and where. It is about who owns the fab, not who designs the chip, and that distinction is the reason the section exists. Almost every AI accelerator company is fabless, so the name printed on a product and the company that made it are rarely the same. The accelerators themselves are in GPUs and in NPUs and TPUs, and the memory stacked alongside them is in Memory and Storage.

The entries are hand-curated rather than harvested, each anchored to a single source URL that is link-checked daily, and all five were verified on September 5, 2026. This is an editorial shortlist, not a fab census. It carries no wafer capacity figures, no yield data, and no per-fab output, so it can tell a reader which companies operate at which end of the market but not how much any of them actually produces. TSMC is a specific case worth flagging: its corporate site blocks automated verification, so its entry is anchored to its SEC 20-F filing index instead.

Five entries, and the concentration they describe is the point. TSMC's entry records that it fabricates nearly every leading AI accelerator, covering NVIDIA, AMD, Apple, and Google TPU parts on N5, N4, and N3 nodes, which means one company's node roadmap sets the ceiling for most of the industry. Samsung Foundry is the only other leading-edge logic option, on gate-all-around SF3 and SF2. Intel Foundry appears as a bid rather than an incumbent, with 18A as its leading-edge offer for AI silicon. GlobalFoundries is here for trailing-edge and specialty work, the US volume foundry for everything that does not need the leading edge, and SMIC as China's domestic fabrication path under export controls. Only two of the five are leading-edge at volume today. What the section does not yet carry is location detail per fab, so it names who manufactures but not where each specific plant sits.

sections.name: Memory and Storage
sections.blurb:
This section covers the memory that sits next to the accelerator and the storage tiers that keep it fed. Those are two quite different businesses held in one list. High bandwidth memory is made by a three-company oligopoly with multi-year supply commitments, while AI storage is a competitive software market where the differentiator is how fast a filesystem can feed thousands of GPUs. The accelerators are in GPUs, and the network that moves data between nodes is in Networking Fabric.

Entries are hand-curated with one source URL each, link-checked daily. Three of the four were verified on September 5, 2026. The Micron entry is dated September 4 and carries an explicit note that the publisher blocks automated checks, so it is confirmed by hand rather than on the daily cycle. The section holds no capacity figures, no pricing, no bandwidth per stack, and no supply share, so it identifies the players and their role but does not quantify any of it. In a market where HBM allocation is the practical constraint on accelerator shipments, that is a real limit on what these entries can tell a reader.

Four entries, split evenly. On memory, SK hynix is recorded as the leading HBM supplier and NVIDIA's primary datacenter memory partner, shipping HBM3E and HBM4, and Micron as the US supplier whose HBM3E ships in H200 and Blackwell platforms. That is two of the three companies making HBM at volume. The third, Samsung, appears on this site under Chip Fabrication for its foundry business rather than here for its memory, so the HBM picture in this section is incomplete by one major supplier. On storage, VAST Data is listed as an all-flash platform deployed in GPU clusters including CoreWeave's, and WEKA as a parallel filesystem for training input and output at hyperscale customers. Nothing in the section covers general DRAM or the SSD tiers the section title mentions.

sections.name: Networking Fabric
sections.blurb:
This section covers the interconnect inside and between training nodes: the scale-up fabric that links GPUs within a rack and the scale-out fabric that links racks into a cluster. Front-end and wide-area networking is out of scope, which matters because networking in a datacenter usually means the front-end network and this section is about the back-end one, where a slow link stalls every GPU in the job. The accelerators themselves are in GPUs, and the building and power around them are in Power and Cooling.

Entries are hand-curated with a single source URL each, link-checked daily, and all five were verified on September 5, 2026. What the section maps is the set of technology choices available, not the market. It carries no port counts, no deployed fabric sizes, no bandwidth benchmarks, and no price per port, so it can tell a reader which options exist and who backs each one but not which is winning by installed base.

Five entries, and their shape is the finding. Two of the five are NVIDIA's. Quantum InfiniBand is recorded as the dominant training-cluster interconnect, with the entry naming the Mellanox acquisition as the source of that position, and NVLink with NVSwitch is the intra-node and rack-scale fabric, where NVL72 puts 72 GPUs into a single NVLink domain. So one vendor supplies both layers of the fabric in a large share of clusters. The other three entries are all the Ethernet route, in different forms. Broadcom's Tomahawk merchant switch silicon, from the 51.2T Tomahawk 5 onward, is what clusters use when they choose Ethernet. Arista supplies switching platforms for hyperscaler AI back-end networks. And the Ultra Ethernet Consortium is the industry effort to close the remaining gap with InfiniBand, with a 1.0 specification published in 2025 and members including AMD, Broadcom, Cisco, Meta, and Microsoft. One incumbent with two products, three routes around it.

sections.name: Power and Cooling
sections.blurb:
This section covers how an AI datacenter gets electricity and gets rid of heat: grid connection and interconnection queues, the generation contracted to serve the load, and the shift from air to liquid cooling that dense GPU racks forced. Individual facilities are in Data Centers, and the racks and interconnect inside them are in the other hardware sections.

The section exists partly to keep four numbers apart that directories routinely print as one another. Critical IT load is the power delivered to the servers themselves. Utility power is the total the facility draws from the grid, which is IT load plus cooling, conversion, and losses, and it is what power usage effectiveness relates to IT load. Standby diesel generation is capacity that exists to ride out an outage and almost never runs. On-site or behind-the-meter generation is dedicated power wired straight to the facility, bypassing a public grid connection. A campus announced as one gigawatt may mean any of the four, and they are nowhere near the same size.

The three named entries here are hand-curated and link-checked daily, all verified on September 5, 2026. The quantitative backing sits elsewhere on the site and refreshes on its own schedule. Interconnection and generation observations are logged from five grid operators and the EIA, and the facility register holds 1,840 datacenters across 397 operators in 8 countries. Only 145 of those 1,840 facilities carry a critical IT megawatt figure, under 8 percent, so any total built from this data is a floor rather than an estimate. The register meant to hold capacity observations tagged by which of the four numbers above they represent is currently empty, so the distinction is defined here but not yet measured facility by facility. Among the curated entries, the Department of Energy one carries the finding that US datacenters used about 4.4 percent of national electricity in 2023, with a projected 6.7 to 12 percent by 2028, a range wide enough to be a statement about uncertainty rather than a forecast.

domains.name: AI Agents and the MCP Ecosystem
domains.blurb: Autonomous and multi-agent systems, planning and memory, tool use, and the Model Context Protocol servers, clients, registries, and security model.

sections.name: Autonomous Agents
sections.blurb:
This section covers single agents that take a goal and run their own loop of planning, tool calls, and self-correction without a person approving each step. The boundary is deliberate. Coordination between several agents belongs in Multi-agent Systems, and agents specialised to write code or drive a browser sit in Coding and Browser Agents. What is listed here is a curated shortlist of open-source projects, not a directory of commercial agent products.

Entries come from GitHub and are refreshed daily by the same pipeline that builds the other repository sections, most recently on September 5, 2026. For each project the section records stars, licence, primary language, whether the repository is archived, and the date of the last push. Star counts are the weakest of those signals. They accumulate over a project's entire life, they never fall when a project is abandoned, and they measure attention rather than production use or code quality. The last push date is the more honest indicator of whether anyone is still working on the code.

The section currently holds four repositories with 332,598 stars between them. AutoGPT dominates at 187,148 stars, more than twice OpenHands at 86,242. Third place shows exactly why stars mislead. gpt-engineer carries 55,106 stars but the repository is archived, its last commit was in May 2025, and its own description points readers to a commercial successor project. Langroid at 4,102 stars is the only small entry. On licensing, three are MIT and one, AutoGPT, is a custom licence, which is the single entry here that a company cannot assume is permissive without reading the terms. Four projects is a thin shortlist for a category this broad, and nothing in it is a commercial or hosted agent platform.

sections.name: Multi-agent Systems
sections.blurb:
This section covers what happens when more than one agent is involved: orchestration frameworks that run a set of agents, delegation patterns that hand work between them, and the wire protocols agents from different vendors use to talk to each other. Single-agent loops are in Autonomous Agents and the persistence layer is in Agent Memory and Planning. Frameworks and protocol specifications are kept in the same list here even though they are different kinds of thing, which is worth knowing before comparing entries side by side.

The list is built from GitHub and refreshed daily, most recently on September 5, 2026, recording stars, licence, primary language, and last push date. Stars are not comparable across the two kinds of entry. A framework's stars roughly track people trying to build with it, while a specification repository's stars track interest in an idea, and an explicitly educational repository collects stars from readers who never ship anything with it.

There are five repositories, 184,172 stars combined. Microsoft's autogen leads at 60,814 with crewAI close behind at 58,109. A2A sits third at 25,637 and is a protocol specification rather than a framework, so its number is a different unit from the two above it. OpenAI's swarm at 21,941 describes itself as an educational framework for exploring orchestration, not a production one, and camel closes the list at 17,671. Maintenance splits the group cleanly. crewAI, A2A, and camel were all pushed within two days of the September 5 refresh, while autogen and swarm both last saw a push in April 2026, roughly five months earlier. Licences are two MIT, two Apache-2.0, and one CC-BY-4.0 on autogen, which is a content licence rather than a software licence and is worth a look before shipping anything built on it.

sections.name: Agent Memory and Planning
sections.blurb:
This section covers the layer that lets an agent carry state across turns and across sessions: storing what happened, retrieving the relevant part of it later, and building the working context an agent plans against. The boundary is narrow on purpose. The agent loop itself is in Autonomous Agents, coordination between agents is in Multi-agent Systems, and general vector databases are treated as infrastructure rather than agent memory. Entries are open-source projects only.

The list is drawn from GitHub and refreshed daily by the same pipeline as the other repository sections, most recently on September 5, 2026. It records stars, licence, primary language, and the date of the last push. A caution specific to this category is that several of these projects are the open-source face of a hosted commercial service, so the repository under a company's name is not always the engine that runs in production. Star counts say nothing about which of the two a reader is looking at.

This is the smallest of the five agent sections, with three repositories and 94,245 stars combined. mem0 holds 64,733 of those, roughly 69 percent of the section total, followed by letta at 24,622 and zep at 4,890. All three are Apache-2.0, making this the only agent section on the site where licensing is unanimous. Two limits are visible in the data. zep's public repository describes itself as examples and integrations rather than the memory engine, which is the hosted-service pattern described above. And despite the section name, all three entries are memory systems. Nothing here is a planner, a task decomposition library, or a recovery and retry framework, so the planning half of the title is currently unpopulated.

sections.name: Coding and Browser Agents
sections.blurb:
This section covers agents that operate a real tool rather than only producing text: agents that read and edit a codebase and run its tests, and agents that drive a browser by clicking, typing, and reading pages. The two are grouped because they share the hard part, which is acting on a live system where a wrong step has consequences. General-purpose agent loops are in Autonomous Agents. Code completion that only suggests text inline is out of scope, as are commercial products without an open repository.

Entries come from GitHub, refreshed daily by the same pipeline as the other repository sections, most recently on September 5, 2026, recording stars, licence, primary language, and last push date. This category moves faster than the site can rank it, so stars lag reality badly here. A project can gain tens of thousands of stars in a quarter, and a heavily used commercial coding agent with no public repository will not appear in this list at all no matter how many people run it daily.

Five repositories, 288,561 stars combined, the largest star total of the five agent sections. browser-use leads at 112,362. The split is two browser agents and three coding agents: browser-use and stagehand at 24,152 on one side, cline at 67,515, aider at 48,763, and continue at 35,769 on the other. Maintenance is unusually current. Four of the five were pushed within a day of the September 5 refresh. The exception is aider, whose last commit was May 22, 2026, more than three months earlier, which is a long gap in a category where model interfaces change every few weeks. Licences are three Apache-2.0 and two MIT, with no custom or restricted terms anywhere in the group.

sections.name: Voice and Service Agents
sections.blurb:
This section covers agents that hold a spoken conversation in real time: the frameworks that stitch together speech recognition, a model, speech synthesis, and a telephony or WebRTC transport tight enough that a caller does not hear the seams. Text-only chat assistants are out of scope, as is speech recognition or synthesis on its own, which belongs with models rather than agents. The section is limited to open-source frameworks with a public repository.

The list comes from GitHub and refreshes daily alongside the other repository sections, most recently on September 5, 2026, recording stars, licence, primary language, and last push date. What none of that captures is the thing that actually decides whether a voice agent works, which is end-to-end latency under real network conditions. No benchmark of that kind is collected here, so the entries can be compared on popularity and maintenance activity but not on the quality of the experience they produce.

Three repositories, 40,372 stars combined. That is the smallest total of the five agent sections by a wide margin, roughly one eighth of Coding and Browser Agents. The three are closely matched rather than dominated by one project: pipecat at 15,240, LiveKit's agents at 14,023, and ten-framework at 11,109. All three were pushed within two days of the September 5 refresh, so unlike several other agent sections here, nothing in this one is stale. Each carries a different licence, BSD-2-Clause, Apache-2.0, and a custom licence on ten-framework. The gap worth naming is scope. Every entry is a builder framework. There are no telephony carriers, no contact centre platforms, and no commercial customer service products in the list, so a reader who came for the service agent vendor landscape will not find it here.
